title: Man's robe (girke, agbada, boubou)
medium: Cotton, native silk (tsamiya); plain weave (strip-weaving); embroidery (button hole, chain, and damask darning (linzami) stitches)
medium_parts: embroidery (button hole, chain, and damask darning (linzami) stitches)
credit_line: Gift of Klaus and Ellen Werner
identifying_description: Made from strip-woven indigo-dyed fabric referred to as saki. The Hausa refer to this style of robe as a girke. The girke differes from the riga, the other style of large robe, by the use of gussets. The girke saki is an important indicator of political and social status. The lining of striped red silk further indicates that this is one of the most prestigious gowns. This robe is embroidered with the Hausa motif, aska takwas (eight knives) in a native silk referred to as tsamiya.
web_text: Throughout Nigeria, prestigious Muslim men from the Hausa, Nupe, and Yoruba tribes adorn themselves with a “robe of honor” or “big robe” at times of important religious or political occasions in order to convey their wealth, social status, and political authority. The Hausa refer to robes with gusset inserts, such as this one, as girke, whereas the Yoruba and Nupe call them agbada, and the majority of French-speaking West Africa refers to them as boubou. This gown is constructed from blue and white strip-woven cloth (saki) produced by the Nupe. It has been embroidered with the popular motif aska takwas or “eight knives” by itinerant Quranic scholars residing in urban centers. Subtle distinctions in the robe's construction from choice of materials to technical qualities convey a complex hierarchy of value. The blue and white saki cloth signifies political authority; however, the presence of a striped cotton lining instead of silk, the embroidery floss of indigenous as opposed to imported silk, and the lack of layering in the embroidery patterns could indicate that the wearer was of high political rank, but not royal lineage.
